**Robust Local‑Only Backup Routine** | **Component** | **What to use** | **Why (wiki source)** | |---|---|---| | **Hardware** | • **Two external drives** – one “weekly” drive (≈1 TB SSD or HDD) and one “monthly” drive (≈2 TB, preferably a different brand/model).
• **Optional third drive** kept at a different location (e.g., a friend’s house) for true off‑site redundancy. | The **Local Backup Strategy** concept recommends a rotating set of external drives to protect against both accidental loss and drive failure [[concepts/local_backup_strategy]]. | | **Backup Tool** | **Windows 11 File History** (built‑in) | Provides automated, versioned copies of selected folders without any cloud dependency [[entities/file_history]], [[entities/windows_11]]. | | **Folder Set to Back Up** | `Documents`, `Pictures`, `Videos`, `Desktop`, and any custom `Projects` folder you create. | Focuses on irreplaceable user data and avoids full system images, as advised in the summary [[summaries/session-12_2024-06-15]]. | | **Schedule** | • **Weekly drive** – plug in **once a week** (e.g., Sunday evening). File History runs automatically (daily frequency, but only when the drive is present).
• **Monthly drive** – swap in **every month** (or every 2‑3 months) and let it get the same daily backup when connected.
• **Optional third drive** – store a copy of the latest monthly backup in a different physical location and update it every 3‑6 months. | The rotating‑drive cadence is the core of the local‑backup approach [[concepts/local_backup_strategy]]. | | **Retention / Versioning** | Set **Backup frequency = Daily** (the smallest interval File History offers). Use the **“until space is needed”** retention policy so older versions are purged automatically, keeping storage simple [[concepts/backup_retention_policy]]. | | | **Best‑Practice Checklist** | 1. **Enable File History** → *Control Panel → System & Security → File History* → *Turn on* (see the step‑by‑step in the session summary).
2. **Add the `Projects` folder** via *Advanced settings → Add folder*.
3. **Label each drive** clearly (e.g., “Backup‑Wk‑2025‑01”, “Backup‑Mo‑2025‑01”).
4. **Store drives separately** – keep the weekly drive near the computer for easy plug‑in, store the monthly drive in a fire‑/water‑resistant box, and the optional third drive off‑site.
5. **Verify restores** at least quarterly: pick a random file, restore it, and check integrity.
6. **Monitor drive health** – run SMART checks or use the OS “Check Disk” utility once a month.
7. **Maintain a shallow, predictable folder hierarchy** (top‑level folders for personal vs. work data) so the set of backed‑up items is obvious and complete [[concepts/folder_hierarchy]]. | These actions tie together the folder‑organization guidance [[summaries/session-12_2024-06-15]] and the local‑backup concept [[concepts/local_backup_strategy]]. | | **Naming & Version Control** | Use **date‑based filenames** (e.g., `2024-09-12_ProjectReport.docx`) and consistent **naming conventions** so that restored files are easy to identify [[concepts/date_based_filenames]], [[concepts/naming_conventions]]. | | ### Quick “Plug‑in” Routine (Weekly) 1. **Connect** the weekly external drive. 2. **Leave the PC on** (or wake it) for a few minutes; File History will detect the drive and start the daily backup. 3. **Eject** the drive safely. 4. **Store** it in its designated drawer. ### Quick “Swap” Routine (Monthly) 1. **Remove** the weekly drive, **plug in** the monthly drive. 2. **Let File History run** (it will copy the same daily backups). 3. **Label** the month on the drive’s case. 4. **Store** the monthly drive in a protected box. --- By following this hardware set‑up, schedule, and checklist you’ll have a **fully offline, low‑maintenance, and redundancy‑rich** backup system that protects your data from device loss, accidental deletion, or drive failure—exactly the kind of solution the knowledge base recommends for users who keep everything locally.

**A smooth move to a new device** (whether it’s a new Windows PC, a Mac, or an iPhone) can be broken into three easy phases that line up with the ways you’ve already been organizing your files: | Phase | What to do | Why it helps (linked to your existing system) | |------|------------|----------------------------------------------| | **1️⃣ Back‑up & capture a snapshot** | • Run **Windows 11 File History** on your current machine (or the equivalent backup on macOS).
• Keep the weekly‑drive copy you already use and also make a fresh copy on a second external drive.
• Verify that the backup contains **all top‑level Personal and Work folders** you’ve created. | Your backup routine from **session‑12 (2024‑06‑15)** already gives you a reliable, rotating‑drive system [[summaries/session-12_2024-06-15]]. Keeping a fresh copy ensures nothing is missed before you de‑provision the old hardware. | | **2️⃣ Replicate the folder hierarchy & naming scheme** | • On the new device, recreate the two‑level **Personal / Work** top‑level folders exactly as they appear in your current tree.
• Inside each, use the same **date‑centric filename pattern**:
`yyyy-mm-dd_description_optional‑project‑or‑client.ext` (lower‑case, dashes, no spaces).
• For work projects, add the three sub‑folders **Admin**, **Notes**, **Outputs** under each `project‑_YYYY` folder. | This matches the lightweight cross‑device hierarchy you defined in **session‑32 (2025‑02‑13)** [[summaries/session-32_2025-02-13]]. Because folder names and filenames avoid spaces/special characters, they sync cleanly to any device (iPhone, iPad, other PCs) [[concepts/cross_device_compatibility]]. | | **3️⃣ Sync & test the new environment** | • Connect the external backup drive to the new device and **restore** the Personal and Work trees (File History on Windows 11, or a manual copy on macOS/Linux).
• Enable a **file‑sync service** you already trust (e.g., iCloud Drive, OneDrive, or a third‑party Sync.com) and point it at the top‑level Personal/Work folders.
• Open a handful of recent files on the new device to confirm they open correctly and that the **date‑based naming** still sorts chronologically. | Using a sync service respects the **cross‑device compatibility** design you built [[concepts/cross_device_compatibility]], and the test step catches any path‑length or permission issues before you fully switch over. | ### Quick checklist you can copy‑paste ``` [ ] Run File History → back up to weekly external drive [ ] Make a second copy on monthly drive (rotate it in) [ ] Verify backup includes: • Personal/ • Work/ [ ] On new device, create: Personal/ Documents/Finance/Taxes/202X … Photos/Family … Work/ Documents/Contracts … Projects/project‑beta_2026/ Admin/ Notes/ Outputs/ [ ] Rename any stray files that don’t follow: yyyy-mm-dd_description[_optional‑context].ext [ ] Connect external drive → restore folders [ ] Enable your preferred file‑sync service → point to top‑level folders [ ] Open 3‑5 recent files → confirm they load & sort correctly [ ] Keep weekly & monthly external drives in rotation for the first month ``` ### How this fits your habit loop * **Consistency** – The same shallow hierarchy and naming convention you already use keeps the mental model unchanged. * **Safety** – Your existing **local backup strategy** (rotating drives + File History) protects you against data loss during the switchover. * **Cross‑device flow** – By avoiding spaces/special characters, the files move smoothly between Windows and iPhone (or any other OS) without renaming headaches. Follow the three phases above and you’ll transition to the new device with minimal friction while keeping everything searchable, version‑controlled, and safely backed up.
